passage: Our final-year project presentation was the first time I tried it for real. Samir went before me and rushed, his voice climbing higher with every slide. When my name was called, I felt the same thing starting: shoulders creeping up, breath stuck high. So I stood at the front, looked at my first slide, and let one long breath out through my nose. I let my shoulders drop. I counted two silent beats. Then I began: "Good morning. I'm Francis, and our project is about rainwater in hostels." My voice came out lower than I expected, and steady. Nobody noticed the pause; the professor later called me "very composed". Samir asked how I stayed calm. I told him it was just one breath, taken before anyone was looking.

qa.a: The project was about rainwater in hostels.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the name was called, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Francis felt nervous; the shoulders crept up and the breath got stuck high.

qa.q: Which steps helped Francis begin steadily?
qa.a: One long exhale through the nose, dropping the shoulders and two silent beats before the first sentence.

qa.q: How might Samir feel hearing that it was just one breath?
qa.a: Samir, who rushed and whose voice climbed, may feel hopeful that the trick is simple enough to learn.

grounding: A student slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence, which steadies voice and thinking without anyone noticing.

passage:
Debate coach's notes, college society. Yogesh Tiwari.
Mahima, second year, opened today's inter-college debate. Last month she rushed her first line and lost her thread. Since then we have practised one thing: reach the podium, breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, and pause before the first word.
Today I watched from the back row. She stepped up, placed her notes, and I saw her shoulders lower. There was a pause, barely a second. Then her first sentence came out clear and unhurried. I doubt anyone else in the hall noticed a thing; they simply heard a confident speaker. She kept her thread through all four minutes, even when heckled.
Next step: I'll ask her to lead a short breathing warm-up for the first-years before the next round.

qa.a: Yogesh watched from the back row.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt stepping up, given what happened last month?
qa.a: Mahima was probably nervous, remembering how she rushed her first line and lost her thread, but she felt prepared.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh plan to have Mahima lead a breathing warm-up?
qa.a: Mahima has shown the routine works, and teaching it lets first-years learn the same quiet steadying before they speak.

qa.q: How did the audience see Mahima's start?
qa.a: They simply heard a confident speaker and most likely did not notice the brief pause at all.

grounding: A student slows the breath, lowers the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence, which steadies the voice without anyone noticing.
